landmarks.name: Ancient City of Palmyra
landmarks.writeup: A UNESCO World Heritage site, Palmyra is an ancient Semitic city with monumental ruins dating back to the Roman Empire.

wiki.extract: Palmyra is an ancient city in central Syria. It is located in the eastern part of the Levant, and archaeological finds date back to the Neolithic period, and documents first mention the city in the early second millennium BCE. Palmyra changed hands on a number of occasions between different empires before becoming a subject of the Roman Empire in the first century CE.

landmarks.name: Umayyad Mosque
landmarks.writeup: Located in Damascus, it is one of the largest and oldest mosques in the world, known for its architectural and religious significance.

wiki.extract: The Umayyad Mosque, also known as the Great Mosque of Damascus, located in the old city of Damascus, the capital of Syria, is one of the largest and oldest mosques in the world. Its religious importance stems from the eschatological reports concerning the mosque and historic events associated with it. Christian and Muslim tradition alike consider it the burial place of John the Baptist's head, a tradition originating in the 6th century. Two shrines inside the premises commemorate the Islamic prophet Muhammad's grandson Husayn ibn Ali, whose martyrdom is frequently compared to that of John the Baptist. It is considered to be the oldest mosque still in use in its original form.

landmarks.name: Citadel of Aleppo
landmarks.writeup: A large medieval fortified palace in Aleppo, representing centuries of military architecture.

wiki.extract: The Citadel of Aleppo is a large medieval fortified palace in the centre of the old city of Aleppo, northern Syria. It is considered to be one of the oldest and largest castles in the world. Usage of the Citadel hill dates back at least to the middle of the 3rd millennium BC. Occupied by many civilizations over time – including the Arameans, Assyrians, Romans, Byzantines, Arabs, Ayyubids, Mamluks and Ottomans – the majority of the construction as it stands today is thought to originate from the Ayyubid period. An extensive conservation work took place in the 2000s by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, in collaboration with Aleppo Archeological Society. Dominating the city, the Citadel is part of the Ancient City of Aleppo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. During the 2010s, the Citadel received significant damage during the lengthy Battle of Aleppo. It was reopened to the public in early 2018 with repairs to damaged parts underway, though some of the damage will be purposefully preserved as part of the history of the citadel. The citadel was damaged by the 2023 Turkey–Syria earthquake.

cultural_events.name: Eid al-Fitr
cultural_events.writeup: A major religious festival marking the end of Ramadan, celebrated with communal prayers and feasts.

wiki.extract: Eid al-Fitr is the first of the two main festivals in Islam, the other being Eid al-Adha. The holiday falls on the first day of Shawwal, the tenth month of the Islamic calendar. One of the most important Islamic celebrations, Eid al-Fitr is celebrated by Muslims worldwide as it marks the end of the month-long, dawn-to-dusk fasting (sawm) during Ramadan. The holiday is known under various other names in different languages and countries around the world.

food_writeup: Syrian cuisine features a rich variety of dishes including kibbeh, hummus, falafel, and baklava, reflecting Levantine culinary traditions with an emphasis on fresh ingredients and spices.
brief_history: Syria has a rich history dating back to ancient civilizations such as the Ebla and Arameans. It was part of various empires including Roman, Byzantine, and Ottoman. Modern Syria gained independence from France in 1946. Since 2011, it has been affected by a complex civil war.

commentary.inflation_management: The IMF data series for Syria covers only 2006-10, when inflation was moderate but volatile: 10.4% in 2006, 15.2% in 2008 on the commodity boom, 4.4% in 2010, under the pound's managed regime. From 2011 the civil war destroyed the monetary system: the pound collapsed from around 47 to the dollar to thousands per dollar on parallel markets, and inflation ran in triple digits in the worst years (not captured in this dataset). There has been no functioning monetary policy for over a decade; dollarization and the war economy set prices.
commentary.debt_management: Recorded public debt fell from 45.0% of GDP in 2006 to 30.0% in 2010 as oil revenues and growth (GDP from $33.8bn to $60.0bn) improved the position. After 2011 there are no IMF data: the war destroyed the oil sector, GDP is estimated to have fallen by more than half, and the state survived on Iranian and Russian support, arrears, and money printing. Any debt figures for the war years would be notional. The fiscal challenge of reconstruction dwarfs anything in the recorded series.

key_events.event: Pre-war period covered by IMF data; moderate growth and falling debt.
Civil war began; IMF data reporting effectively ceased.
War devastated the economy; currency collapsed and sanctions tightened.
Russian military intervention changed the war's course.
Caesar Act sanctions and the Lebanese banking crisis crushed the pound further.
Assad regime fell in December; a transitional government faced economic ruin.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: Syria's outlook depends on political stabilization that is far from assured: reconstruction needs are estimated in the hundreds of billions of dollars against a shattered state. Sanctions relief, refugee return, and oil-field control are the swing factors. Analytical assessment must be heavily caveated: the IMF has no data since 2010, the economy is largely informal and dollarized, and outcomes range from slow rebuilding to renewed fragmentation. No quantitative claims beyond 2010 can be grounded in this dataset.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
